text: Kleisli arrows. An at-do function takes plain values and returns a program.
Calling add one with forty-one runs nothing. It returns a Call node, which is an Expand.
run evaluates the node. Only now does the body run, and forty-two comes back.
The node is a value. Run it again, and the body runs again.
There are two phases. Python builds the program when you call, and the VM runs it later.
Building consults no handler. greeting is built with no handler anywhere.
Running it needs one. With no handler, its Ask is an unhandled effect.
Under reader, the same program runs, and returns Hello, Ada.
That is why a call is a macro, not an effect. An effect would need handlers before the program even exists.
Arguments are passed as given. An effect or a program you pass in stays a value.
echo of Ask x returns the Ask itself, even though x is annotated int.
To use a result, yield it. use values yields both arguments, and gets five and ten.
The usual style: yield in the caller, then pass the plain value on.
There is no map, no flat map. Programs compose by yielding programs inside at-do functions.
fetch user posts yields fetch user of seven. Its value comes back at that yield.
The Ask inside fetch user travels out past both functions, to the reader around the whole run.
Then fetch posts runs the same way, and the outer function returns the posts.
A handler is an at-do function too. The handler decorator makes a function of effect and k into one.
It must take the effect and k. With one parameter, it is refused with a TypeError.
Its annotation must name an effect class. No effect can be an int, so that one is refused too.
Both are refused when the handler is built, before any program runs. fetcher keeps the contract, and answers Fetch.
Plain values in, a program out. Handlers give its effects their meaning. That is a Kleisli arrow in doeff.
